title: The Case for Quiet Cities
summary: Ama and Carlos discuss how constant urban noise affects concentration and wellbeing, and what ordinary people can do about it.

cover.scene: Flat 2D illustration: Ama and Carlos sitting on a rooftop terrace at dusk, city skyline softly glowing behind them, one holding a cup, no text

sentences.text: Carlos, I moved to the city centre last month, and I honestly cannot concentrate with all this traffic.
You are not imagining it, Ama, because constant noise places a surprising strain on the brain.
But I thought people simply got used to it after a while.
Partly, yes, but studies suggest that long exposure still raises stress levels even when you stop noticing the sound.
So my body is reacting even when my mind has switched off?
Precisely, and that is why chronic noise is linked to poor sleep and a kind of background fatigue.
That would explain why I feel exhausted by four in the afternoon.
It might, and it is an effect that many city planners still overlook when they design busy streets.
I suppose we tend to treat noise as an annoyance rather than a health issue.
Exactly, and that attitude is slowly beginning to change.

sentences.text: So what can an ordinary person do, apart from moving to the countryside?
You can start by creating a small sanctuary at home, a room where you deliberately keep things quiet.
I could insulate the window, although that sounds expensive.
Not necessarily, because thick curtains and a few rugs can reduce the echo surprisingly well.
And what about when I am walking outside, where I cannot control anything?
Try choosing a route through a park, since even a short green stretch makes the walk far more pleasant.
That is a lovely idea, and it would give me a reason to walk more.
It would, and some people also schedule ten silent minutes each day, with no phone and no music.
Ten minutes of silence feels almost radical in a city like this.
Perhaps, but it may be the cheapest form of rest you will ever find.
